results.question: According to “A new clump-based star formation model for galaxy simulations: implications for high-redshift compact star clusters”, how does increasing disc compactness (ξ) from 0 to 10 in 10^10 M☉ haloes affect (a) the maximum gas clump mass and surface density, (b) the fraction of clumps exceeding a surface density threshold Σc,th = 300 M☉ pc^-2, and (c) the global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn? Please answer with the quantitative values reported in the paper.
results.reference_answer:
(a) Maximum clump mass increases from ≈ 10^5.1 M☉ at ξ = 0 to ≈ 10^7.4 M☉ at ξ = 10; maximum clump surface density increases from ≈ 10^2.9 M☉ pc^-2 to > 10^4.0 M☉ pc^-2. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(b) The fraction of clumps with Σc ≥ 300 M☉ pc^-2 rises from 0.25 at ξ = 0 to 0.34 at ξ = 6 and 0.38 at ξ = 10. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(c) The global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn increases monotonically from 5 × 10^-3 at ξ = 0 to 2 × 10^-1 at ξ = 10 (for the 10^10 M☉ haloes). (evidence_id: 160dd9270d4a618cf6df643a)

retrieved_chunks.text: We develop a new star formation model for galaxy simulations in which star-forming gas clumps are identified on-the-fly and converted into stars with an efficiency _𝜖_ SF set by the clump surface density Σc, calibrated against radiation hydrodynamics simulations of star cluster formation. Applying this model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[[11]] M⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift _𝑧_ = 0–10, we find that more compact discs form more massive and denser clumps. The maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] to ∼ 10[7] M⊙, and the fraction of clumps exceeding the surface density of 300 M⊙⊙ pc[[−][2]][[2]] rises from 0 _._ 25 to 0 _._ 38 between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes. Star formation becomes correspondingly bursty, and the global star formation efficiency after three disc rotations increases from 5 × 10[−][3] to 2 × 10[−][1] in 10[[10]] M⊙⊙ haloes and from 2 × 10 × 10 10[[−][2]][[2]] to 4 × 10 × 10 10[[−][1]][[1]] in 10[[11]] M⊙⊙ haloes as the redshift increases from _𝑧_ = 0 to 10. The accompanying feedback disrupts the gas discs of the most compact systems, while prominent stellar spiral arms emerge. Self-gravitationally bound star clusters form only in compact discs. We find no bound star clusters at _𝑧_ ≤ 2 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes, whereas the bound cluster mass fraction reaches ≈ ≈ 40 per cent at _𝑧_ ≥ 8 and ≈ ≈ 70 per cent in the most compact 10[11] M⊙ halo.

## **5 CONCLUSION** 

We have investigated how the compactness of galactic discs regulates clumpy star formation and the formation of bound star clusters. To this end, we have developed a new star formation model (CSF) in which star-forming gas clumps are identified on-the-fly and converted into stars with an efficiency _𝜖_ SF set by the clump surface density Σc, calibrated against the radiation hydrodynamics simulations of Fukushima & Yajima (2021). We apply the model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[11] M⊙ with a fixed gas-to-halo mass ratio of 0 _._ 01, adopting disc scale radii 

appropriate for _𝑧_ = 0–10 as a proxy for compactness. Our main results are summarised as follows. 

(i) Compact discs form more massive and denser gas clumps. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] _[.]_[1] to 10[7] _[.]_[4] M⊙ and the maximum clump surface density from ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[9] to _>_ 10[4] _[.]_[0] M⊙ pc[−][2] between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10. The fraction of clumps exceeding Σc _,_ th = 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] rises from 0 _._ 25 at _𝑧_ = 0 to 0 _._ 34 at _𝑧_ = 6 and 0 _._ 38 at _𝑧_ = 10, and the most compact discs host clumps with _𝜖_ SF ∼ 1.

This quantity is the key parameter that determines the star formation efficiency of each clump (see Sec. 2.3.2). Although the PDFs in all simulations peak at ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[3] M⊙ pc[−][2] , the distributions of Σc show a systematic dependence on galactic compactness. In particular, the maximum surface densities increase significantly towards higher _𝑧_ , reaching ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[9] , 10[3] _[.]_[9] , and _>_ 10[4] _[.]_[0] M⊙ pc[−][2] for the _𝑧_ = 0, 6, and 10 simulations, respectively. The fractions of gas clumps with surface densities above the threshold value of Σc _,_ th = 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] , above which the star formation efficiency exceeds ∼ 10 per cent, are ∼ 0 _._ 25, 0 _._ 34, and 0 _._ 38 for the _𝑧_ = 0, 6, and 10 simulations, respectively. These results indicate that gas clumps become systematically denser and more compact in higher- _𝑧_ galaxies, leading to conditions favourable for efficient star formation.

Up to _𝑡_ ≈ _𝑡_ dyn, the high- _𝑧_ galaxies show strong SFR peaks whose amplitudes increase with galactic compactness. ## _2.3.2 Conversion of gas to stars_ 

Once GMCs are identified in our simulations every Δ _𝑇_ c = 1 Myr, we compute the star formation efficiency, _𝜖_ SF, following Yajima (2025) for self-gravitating GMCs ( _𝛼_ vir _<_ 2). The functional form of _𝜖_ SF is given by 

**==> picture [244 x 51] intentionally omitted <==**

where _𝑎_ = 38 _._ 1, _𝜖_ ff _,_ 0 _._ 02 = _𝜖_ ff/0 _._ 02, _𝑇_ HII _,_ 4 = _𝑇_ HII /10[4] K, and Σc _,_ 100 = Σc/100 M⊙ pc[−][2] . In this work, the star formation efficiency per freefall time is fixed to _𝜖_ ff = 0 _._ 02, and the HII region temperature is assumed to be _𝑇_ HII = 10[4] K, since stars are inefficiently formed in gas ionised by stellar radiation when Σc _<_ 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] (Fukushima & Yajima 2021). With these assumptions, Eq. 8 depends only on the GMC surface density, Σc. 

This prescription reproduces the increase in star formation efficiency with increasing cloud surface density found by Fukushima & Yajima (2021). For Σc _<_ 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] , _𝜖_ SF remains at the level of a few per cent or less, reflecting efficient disruption of GMCs by photoionisation feedback. In contrast, for Σc ≥ 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] , _𝜖_ SF increases to values of order a few tens of per cent, corresponding to continued star formation in compact, gravitationally bound clouds where feedback is less effective at dispersing the gas. This behaviour is motivated by the picture that star formation in GMCs proceeds until radiation pressure becomes comparable to the self-gravity of the forming star cluster.

Such bursty star formation drives strong stellar feedback, injecting large amounts of energy into the surrounding ISM and ultimately disrupting the gaseous structures, as shown in Fig. 1. Such bursty star formation may also be relevant to the statistical properties of high- _𝑧_ galaxies revealed by JWST. The unexpectedly high abundance of UV-luminous galaxies at _𝑧_ ≳ 10 (e.g. Harikane et al. 2023) has been attributed in part to stochastic star formation, which scatters galaxies to brighter magnitudes and boosts the observed UV luminosity function. Our model produces such burstiness self-consistently from cloud-scale physics, and thus provides a physically motivated origin for the scatter required by these interpretations. 

The bottom panel of Fig. 3 shows the evolution of the total stellar mass formed during the simulations. In all cases, the stellar mass growth largely saturates by _𝑡_ ≈ _𝑡_ dyn. Given the initial gas disc mass of _𝑀_ d = 10[8] M⊙, the galactic star formation efficiencies at _𝑡_ = 3 _𝑡_ dyn, defined as SFE = _𝑀★_ ( _𝑡_ = 3 _𝑡_ dyn)/ _𝑀_ d, are approximately 5 × 10[−][3] , 2 × 10[−][2] , 5 × 10[−][2] , 1 × 10[−][1] , 1 × 10[−][1] , and 2 × 10[−][1] for _𝑧_ = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10, respectively. These results indicate that galactic star formation becomes substantially more efficient in compact high- _𝑧_ galaxies.
